title: The longest drinking straw
hook: A perfect pump on a very tall straw. How high can it lift the water?

knows: you drink through a straw by sucking
doesNotKnow: that suction does not pull: the air pressing on the open water pushes it up the straw
that this push can hold only about 10 m of water

misconception: With a strong enough pump you can suck water up a straw of any height.
objective: The learner can explain that a pump only removes air, and that the air pressing on the open water pushes the water up, so at sea level the column can be at most about 10 m tall (less under thinner air).

claims.text: A column of liquid held up by a pressure difference ΔP has height h = ΔP/(ρ g); with air pressing on the open water and only water vapour above the column, the push can hold up only about 10 m of water (stage: the column stopping on the 0-14 m scale with 'no air' above it; reveal: 'that push can hold up only about 10 m of water').
claims.source: Hydrostatics: P_atm − P_top = ρ g h. artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (block '65 longest-drinking-straw'). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, chapter on fluids. Brief #67 claim 1.

'About 10 m' matches. Source fix: replace the unopened Halliday citation with m42195 and m42192.

claims.text: At standard sea-level pressure (101,325 Pa), with water at 20 °C (vapour pressure about 2.34 kPa, density 998 kg/m³), the column reaches 10.1 m (10.3 m if vapour is ignored), so a 5 m straw fills to the top and a 12 m straw stops at 10.1 m (stage: column readout and Seen row '5 m: top · 12 m: stops at 10.1 m'; caption 'Perfect pump, 20 °C water.'; reveal: 'In your 5 m straw the water reached the top, but in the 12 m straw it stopped at 10.1 m, with empty space above').
claims.source: (101,325 − 2,339) / (998 × 9.81) = 10.11 m; 101,325 / (998 × 9.81) = 10.35 m. artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (h_withVapour_m 10.11, h_ideal_m 10.35). Standard atmosphere 101,325 Pa; vapour pressure of water at 20 °C from the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (table of vapour pressure of water). Demo.tsx hMax(). Brief #67 claim 2.

claims.text: Air pressure on the summit of Everest is about 33.7 kPa, so there the column holds only 3.2 m (stage: thinner air arrows, column readout and Seen row 'Everest: 3.2 m'; reveal: 'On Everest, under thinner air, it held just 3.2 m').
claims.source: West, J. B., 'Barometric pressures on Mt. Everest: new data and physiological significance', Journal of Applied Physiology 86 (1999). (33,700 − 2,339) / (998 × 9.81) = 3.20 m: artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (Everest summit h_withVapour_m 3.2). Cross-check in the brief: an isothermal atmosphere (scale height about 7.4 km) gives about 31 kPa, also about 3 m. Brief #67 claim 3.

Own: (33,730 - 2,339)/(998*9.81) = 3.21 m; at 251 Torr 3.18 m; both 3.2 m to 1 dp. 'About 33.7 kPa' and 3.2 m hold. Water kept at 20 C on Everest is a stated idealisation (c5).

claims.text: Suction does not pull water: the pump only removes air from the straw, and the air pressing on the water in the glass pushes it up into the region of lower pressure (stage: 'air pushes' arrows on the open water, the pump drawn at the top; reveal: 'Suction does not pull water. The pump only removes air from the straw; the air pressing on the water in the glass pushes it up').
claims.source: A fluid cannot sustain the tension a 'pull' would need here; the net force on the column is the pressure difference between its bottom (air pressure through the open water) and its top (near-vacuum). Same fluids chapter. Brief #67 claim 4.
claims.note: FC wj64 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2 [project:wave-j], W-1490, main 0027f27+): VERIFIED. m42195: in the barometer 'The atmosphere is able to force mercury in the tube to a height h because the pressure above the mercury is zero'; the same push explains the straw: the net force on the column is the pressure difference, supplied by the air on the open water. Reveal sentence matches. Source fix: the source line says 'A fluid cannot sustain the tension a pull would need'; that is too strong (water can sustain metastable tension in clean narrow tubes and plant xylem). Suggest 'in an ordinary straw, dissolved gas and nucleation sites prevent the water from holding tension'. The learner-facing sentence is fine under c5's idealisation.

claims.text: Idealisations: a perfect pump that leaves only water vapour above the column, water at 20 °C, a rigid straw, no dissolved gas coming out of the water. The 0-14 m scale is drawn compressed (12.6 px per m) and the air arrows are schematic (thinner on Everest).
claims.source: Stated assumption, brief #67 claim 5. Demo.tsx: PX_PER_M 12.6; arrow width 3 px at sea level, 1.4 px on Everest. The caption 'Perfect pump, 20 °C water.' states the main assumptions on the stage.

recall.question: A pump at the top of a 15 m well cannot lift the water, but one at the bottom can. Why?
options: The air can push water up only about 10 m; a pump at the bottom pushes
A pump at the top is too far from the water to suck it
Water gets heavier the higher it is lifted
recall.why: A pump at the top only removes air; the atmosphere's push holds up at most about 10 m of water. A pump at the bottom pushes the water up itself.
